::: {.why}
Smoothed returns are the easiest way to look good without doing anything, and it happens accidentally in illiquid holdings as often as it happens deliberately.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Give the correction to an annualised Sharpe ratio for autocorrelated returns, and evaluate it for a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.2.
- Name two mechanisms that produce positive return autocorrelation without any skill, and say which one you might introduce accidentally.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Derive the corrected annualisation factor: the variance of a sum of correlated returns includes the covariance terms, so the naive square root of 252 is wrong. Write the general factor for an arbitrary autocorrelation function, then simplify for AR(1) and evaluate at rho of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Demonstrate the inflation: take a return series with zero true autocorrelation, apply a two-period moving average to it, and compute the naive annualised Sharpe of the smoothed series against the original. Report the inflation factor. Then note that a monthly-marked illiquid position produces the same effect for free.
:::
:::
